title: Introduction to Anatomical Terms & Body Organisation
summary: The language of anatomy — positions, planes, movement terms and how the body is organised from cell to system.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words Anatomy needs a fixed starting position so that "above" and "left" mean the same thing to everyone. That position is the anatomical position : standing upright, face forward, arms by the side, palms facing forward, feet together. From that position we describe the body using planes, directions and movement words. Learn these first — every later chapter uses them. Key points Levels of organisation: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. Four tissue types: epithelial (covering), connective (support), muscular (movement), nervous (control). title: Circulatory & Lymphatic System
summary: The heart, blood vessels and lymphatics — how blood is pumped, where it travels and how tissue fluid is drained.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist, lying behind the sternum with its apex pointing to the left. It pushes blood through two loops: - Pulmonary circulation — heart → lungs → heart (picks up oxygen). - Systemic circulation — heart → body → heart (delivers oxygen and food). Blood never flows backwards because four valves act as one-way doors. title: Digestive System
summary: The mouth-to-anus tube and its helper organs, and how food is broken down and absorbed.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words Digestion breaks large food molecules into small ones that can pass into the blood. It happens along one long tube — about 9 metres from mouth to anus — helped by three organs: the liver , gall bladder and pancreas . Food is pushed along by peristalsis , wave-like contractions of smooth muscle. The inner lining of the small intestine has finger-like folds called villi , which greatly increase the surface for absorption. title: Endocrine System
summary: The ductless glands, the hormones they release and the body functions they control.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words Endocrine glands have no ducts. They pour hormones straight into the blood, and the blood carries them to target cells. A hormone is a chemical messenger that switches a body process on or off. Hormone levels are kept steady by negative feedback : when the level of a hormone rises, it switches off its own production. For example, high thyroid hormone tells the pituitary to stop making TSH. summary: Bones, joints and muscles — the skeleton's framework, types of joints and how skeletal muscle moves the body.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words The musculoskeletal system gives the body its shape, supports it and allows movement. Bones act as levers, joints act as hinges, and muscles pull on bones to move them. Bone is living tissue — constantly broken down and rebuilt. A break in a bone is called a fracture . Bones store calcium and make blood cells in the red bone marrow. title: Nervous System
summary: The brain, spinal cord and nerves — central and peripheral nervous system and their main functions.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words The nervous system controls and coordinates everything the body does. It has two main parts: - Central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord. It receives information, makes decisions and sends instructions. - Peripheral nervous system (PNS) — all the nerves that run from the CNS to the body. It carries messages in both directions. The basic working cell is the neuron : a cell body, dendrites that receive signals, and an axon that sends them. Many axons are wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath , which speeds up the signal. summary: The kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra — how urine is formed and how the body controls water and salt balance.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words The urinary system removes waste products and excess water and salts from the blood. The two kidneys filter the blood, make urine, and help control blood pressure and pH. The ureters carry urine to the bladder, which stores it until the urethra releases it. A healthy adult makes about 1–2 litres of urine per day , and normal urine output is 0.5–1 mL per kg per hour . summary: The organs that bring air in and out, and the tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words Breathing is not the same as respiration. Breathing (ventilation) moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the whole process: taking in oxygen, using it in cells, and removing carbon dioxide. Air travels along one road: Nose → Pharynx → Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli The lungs do not have muscles of their own. summary: The eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin — how the body receives light, sound, smell, taste and touch.
subject: Applied Anatomy
text: In simple words Sensory organs turn one kind of energy into nerve impulses. The eye turns light into sight, the ear turns sound waves into hearing and also senses balance, the nose detects chemicals for smell, the tongue detects them for taste, and the skin senses touch, heat, cold and pain. title: Blood
summary: Blood composition, plasma, red and white cells, platelets, blood groups and clotting.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words Blood is a connective tissue that carries oxygen, food, hormones and waste around the body, defends against infection and stops bleeding after injury. About 55% of blood is plasma and 45% is formed elements (cells and platelets). An adult has about 5 litres of blood . Blood has a slightly alkaline pH of about 7.35–7.45. title: Circulatory & Lymphatic System
summary: How the heart pumps blood, the cardiac cycle, blood pressure regulation and lymphatic return.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words The heart pumps blood around the body in a repeating sequence called the cardiac cycle . Each heartbeat has two phases: - Systole — the chambers contract and push blood out. - Diastole — the chambers relax and fill with blood. The two heart sounds ("lub-dub") come from the valves closing: "lub" when the AV valves close at the start of ventricular systole; "dub" when the semilunar valves close at the end. Cardiac output Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume Normal values: - Heart rate: 60–100 beats/minute at rest - Stroke volume: about 70 mL per beat - Cardiac output: about 5 litres/minute Stroke volume is the amount of blood ejected by one ventricle in one beat. Blood pressure Blood pressure is the force of blood against artery walls: - Systolic — pressure during ventricular contraction (normally about 120 mmHg). - Diastolic — pressure during relaxation (normally about 80 mmHg). - Pulse pressure — systolic minus diastolic (normally 30–50 mmHg). title: Digestive System
summary: How food is digested and absorbed — enzymes, bile, peristalsis and the liver's metabolic role.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words Digestion turns food into tiny particles that can pass into the blood. It uses both mechanical digestion (chewing and churning) and chemical digestion (enzymes that split large molecules into small ones). Each enzyme has a specific job — amylase for starch, protease for protein, lipase for fat. None of them work outside their best pH, which is why stomach acid and intestinal alkali both matter. title: General Physiology & Cell Physiology
summary: How cells build themselves, move substances across membranes and hold the internal environment steady — the foundation of all nursing science.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words Every patient you care for is a collection of about 30 trillion cells, and each cell is a tiny factory surrounded by a fence. The fence is the cell membrane . It decides what comes in and what goes out — water, oxygen, glucose, sodium, waste. If the fence fails, the cell swells, stops working and dies. Inside the cell, the nucleus holds DNA and gives orders. Mitochondria burn glucose with oxygen to make ATP , the cell’s energy currency. Ribosomes build proteins, the endoplasmic reticulum folds and ships them, and the Golgi apparatus packs them for delivery. Lysosomes are the recycling bins. The body also keeps a steady internal state called homeostasis : temperature near 37 °C, blood pH 7.35–7.45, glucose 70–110 mg/dL, and fluid balance within tight limits. Every illness is, in one way or another, a failure of homeostasis — and every nursing action aims to restore it. The cell membrane and its transport The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer : water-loving heads face outwards, fatty tails face inwards. Proteins float within it as channels, carriers and pumps. title: Musculoskeletal System
summary: How bone grows and repairs, how muscle contracts, and how joints move the body.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words Bone is living tissue that grows, repairs itself and stores calcium. Muscle contracts by sliding filaments past each other, pulling on bones through tendons. Joints allow movement in different amounts depending on their type. Calcium and vitamin D are essential for strong bones. Weight-bearing exercise keeps bones dense. Bone physiology Bone is constantly remodelled: - Osteoblasts build new bone. - Osteoclasts break down old bone. - Osteocytes are mature bone cells. Fracture repair happens in stages: bleeding forms a haematoma , a soft callus forms, then hard bone replaces it. Healing takes weeks to months and needs good blood supply, nutrition and immobilisation. A long bone grows in length at the epiphyseal plate (growth plate). Growth stops when the plate closes after puberty. Muscle contraction Skeletal muscle has actin (thin) and myosin (thick) filaments. When stimulated, myosin heads pull actin filaments inward — the sliding filament theory . This shortens the muscle and pulls the bone. Energy comes from ATP . title: Renal System
summary: How the kidneys form urine, control water, salt, acid–base balance and blood pressure.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words The kidneys filter the blood, remove waste, and control water, salt and acid–base balance. Each kidney has about one million nephrons, and each nephron forms urine by three steps: 1. Filtration — blood is filtered in the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule. 2. Reabsorption — useful substances (glucose, amino acids, most water and salts) are taken back into the blood. 3. Secretion — extra wastes and ions are added to the tubule from the blood. Normal urine is about 95% water and 5% wastes . Normal output is 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour ; urine specific gravity is about 1.010–1.025 . The nephron Each nephron has a glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule, then the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. - Proximal tubule — reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids and most water and sodium. - Loop of Henle — concentrates the urine. - Distal tubule — fine-tunes sodium, potassium and pH under hormone control. - Collecting duct — final water adjustment under ADH; carries urine to the renal pelvis. subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words This chapter covers two control systems. The reproductive system is controlled by hormones from the hypothalamus, pituitary and gonads, producing the menstrual cycle in females and sperm continuously in males. The nervous system uses electrical impulses along neurons and chemical signals across synapses. It senses, integrates and responds — the somatic system for voluntary movement and the autonomic system for involuntary body functions. title: Respiratory System
summary: How the lungs move air, exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, and keep blood gases within the narrow range the body can tolerate.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words The lungs are two soft bags hanging in a sealed box. The box is the chest, and its floor is the diaphragm . When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the box gets bigger, pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure, and air rushes in. When the diaphragm relaxes, the box shrinks and air flows out. That is all quiet breathing is. Inside the lungs, air reaches about 300 million tiny sacs called alveoli . Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries, and the wall between air and blood is less than one micrometre thick. Oxygen crosses into the blood, carbon dioxide crosses out. The total alveolar surface is roughly 70 square metres — about half a tennis court folded into your chest. Physiology matters clinically because the lungs do two jobs at once: they bring oxygen in and they control the body’s acid level by blowing off carbon dioxide. A patient who breathes too slowly retains CO₂ and turns acidotic; a patient who breathes too fast washes CO₂ out and turns alkalotic. Mechanics of breathing Inspiration is active. title: Special Senses
summary: How the eye sees, the ear hears and balances, and the nose and tongue detect smell and taste.
subject: Applied Physiology
text: In simple words Special senses turn one kind of energy into nerve impulses that the brain interprets. The eye turns light into sight, the ear turns sound into hearing (and also senses balance), and the nose and tongue detect chemicals for smell and taste. The eye has a focusing system (cornea and lens) and a sensing layer (retina). The ear has a collecting part, a middle-ear amplifier, and an inner-ear sensory part. Vision Light passes: cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous humour → retina . - The cornea and lens refract (bend) light so it focuses on the retina. - The iris changes the pupil size to control how much light enters. - Accommodation is the lens changing shape to focus near or far objects. - Rods work in dim light (black and white); cones work in bright light (colour). - The optic nerve carries signals to the visual cortex. Common errors: - Myopia (short sight): image focuses in front of the retina; corrected with a concave lens. - Hypermetropia (long sight): image focuses behind the retina; corrected with a convex lens. title: Introduction to Psychology
summary: What psychology is, its goals and branches, and why it matters for nursing care.
subject: Applied Psychology
text: In simple words Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Behaviour is anything a person does that can be observed; mental processes are thoughts, feelings, memories and perceptions that happen inside. The goals of psychology are to describe, explain, predict and control behaviour — to understand why people act as they do and to help them change when needed. Nursing is about people, so psychology helps nurses understand patients' fears, reactions to illness, pain and stress, and to communicate better. title: Mental Health & Mental Hygiene
summary: What mental health means, signs of good and poor mental health, and how to promote it.
subject: Applied Psychology
text: In simple words Mental health is a state of well-being in which a person can cope with normal stress, work productively and contribute to the community. It is not just the absence of mental illness. Mental hygiene means the habits and practices that keep the mind healthy — managing stress, expressing feelings, sleeping well and seeking help early. Mental illness is a diagnosable condition that disturbs thinking, feeling or behaviour and reduces a person's ability to cope. Common examples are anxiety, depression and schizophrenia. Signs of good mental health - Realistic self-esteem and confidence - Ability to form and keep relationships - Can cope with stress and bounce back - Makes decisions and solves problems - Feels in control of life - Shows appropriate emotions Factors affecting mental health - Biological — genes, brain chemistry, hormones - Psychological — coping style, self-esteem, past trauma - Social — family support, finances, housing, culture - Environmental — workplace stress, disasters, violence Early warning signs of poor mental health: withdrawal, mood swings, sleep change, poor concentration, irritability, hopelessness, substance misuse. title: Motivation & Emotional Processes
summary: Motivation theories, emotions, stress and coping — how they affect patient behaviour and recovery.
subject: Applied Psychology
text: In simple words Motivation is what drives behaviour toward a goal. Emotion is a feeling state such as fear, joy or anger. Stress is the body's response to demands; coping is how a person manages it. Nurses meet patients who are frightened, in pain or stressed — understanding motivation and emotion helps them care better. Maslow's hierarchy of needs Level Need Example --- --- --- 1 Physiological Air, food, water, sleep 2 Safety Security, freedom from fear 3 Love and belonging Family, friends, relationships 4 Esteem Respect, achievement, confidence 5 Self-actualisation Reaching one's potential Lower needs must be mostly met before higher needs become urgent. A patient gasping for breath (physiological) cannot focus on self-esteem. Emotions Basic emotions include happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust. Emotions have three parts: - Physical changes (heart rate, hormones) - Behaviour (facial expression, action) - Feeling (how it is experienced) Stress and coping Stress is the body's response to a threat or demand. title: Personality

subject: Applied Psychology
text: In simple words Personality is the relatively stable pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviour that makes each person unique. It shapes how a person responds to illness, pain, treatment and nurses. Examiners often ask about Freud's structural model and about type/trait approaches. title: Psychological Assessment & Tests
summary: How psychological assessment is done — interviews, observation, tests and what nurses should know.
subject: Applied Psychology
text: In simple words Psychological assessment gathers information about a person's thinking, feeling and behaviour to understand problems and plan help. It uses interviews, observation, questionnaires and standard tests. Nurses do not diagnose mental illness — they observe, record, report and refer to the psychologist or psychiatrist. They also support patients through testing. title: Self-Empowerment
summary: Self-awareness, self-esteem, assertiveness and stress management for personal and professional growth.
subject: Applied Psychology
text: In simple words Self-empowerment means understanding yourself, valuing yourself and speaking up for yourself respectfully. For nurses, it supports confidence, good boundaries and resilience against burnout. Self-awareness is knowing your own feelings, strengths and limits. Self-esteem is how much you value yourself. Assertiveness is expressing your needs clearly while respecting others. Communication styles Style Behaviour Example --- --- --- Passive Gives in, avoids conflict "Whatever you want" Aggressive Pushes own views, ignores others "Do it my way" Assertive States own needs, respects others "I need a break; let's cover each other" Assertive communication uses "I" statements: "I feel…, I need…, I would like…". summary: Soft skills for nurses — communication, teamwork, empathy, time management and professional behaviour.
subject: Applied Psychology
text: In simple words Soft skills are the personal and social skills that help a nurse work well with patients, families and the team. Technical knowledge matters, but soft skills make the difference between good and great care. Key soft skills: communication, empathy, teamwork, time management, stress management and professional behaviour. Key soft skills Skill What it means --- --- Communication Clear speaking, listening and body language Empathy Understanding and sharing the patient's feelings Active listening Fully focusing on what the patient says Teamwork Working with doctors, aides and other nurses Time management Prioritising tasks and using time well Professional behaviour Punctuality, honesty, boundaries, confidentiality Empathy vs sympathy - Empathy — understand the patient's feeling ("I can see this is hard for you"). - Sympathy — feel sorry for the patient ("I feel sorry for you"). title: Clinical Sociology
summary: Applying sociology in health care — the patient as a social person, the hospital as a social system, and the sick role.
subject: Applied Sociology
text: In simple words Clinical sociology applies sociology to health care. It sees the patient not just as a body with disease, but as a social person with family, work, culture and beliefs. The hospital is a social system with its own hierarchy, roles and rules. Understanding it helps nurses work better and help patients cope. The patient as a social person Illness affects more than the body: - Work and income may be lost. - Family roles change (a breadwinner may become dependent). - Relationships may be strained. - The patient may feel stigma or shame. The sick role (Talcott Parsons) Right Obligation --- --- Excused from normal duties Try to get well Not responsible for illness Seek competent help Receive care Co-operate with treatment The sick role is temporary. Problems arise when a patient does not want to give up the role or refuses to accept being ill. The hospital as a social system - Hierarchy: matron, doctors, nurses, aides, cleaners — each with a role. - Rules: visiting hours, shifts, documentation. - Communication: handovers, case notes, rounds. - The patient enters as a stranger and must learn the hospital's rules. title: Culture
summary: Culture, its components, cultural diversity and cultural competence in nursing care.
subject: Applied Sociology
text: In simple words Culture is the shared beliefs, values, customs, language and way of life of a group of people. It is learned and passed from one generation to the next. Culture affects what people eat, how they see illness, what treatment they accept, how they express pain and who makes decisions in the family. Cultural competence means respecting and adapting care to each patient's culture. Components of culture Component Meaning Health example --- --- --- Beliefs Ideas accepted as true Belief that illness is punishment Values Ideas of right and wrong Value of family decision-making Customs Traditional practices Diet during illness or pregnancy Language Way of communicating Patient may not speak the nurse's language Symbols Objects with meaning Religious symbols worn by patients Ethnocentrism and cultural relativism - Ethnocentrism — judging another culture by your own standards ("my way is right"). - Cultural relativism — understanding a culture on its own terms. Nurses must avoid ethnocentrism and respect the patient's cultural beliefs, even when different from their own. title: Family & Marriage
summary: Types of family and marriage, family functions and the family’s role in health and illness.
subject: Applied Sociology
text: In simple words The family is the basic unit of society. It is the first place where a person learns values, behaviour and attitudes toward health. Families come in many forms — nuclear, joint and extended — and each affects how a patient is cared for at home. Marriage is a socially approved union between two people. Its forms vary across cultures and religions. Types of family Type Meaning --- --- Nuclear family Parents and their children Joint family Parents, children, grandparents, uncles, aunts living together Extended family Nuclear family plus other relatives nearby Single-parent family One parent with children In India, the joint family is common and gives strong support, but it can also mean many people are involved in decisions. Types of marriage - Monogamy — one husband, one wife. - Polygamy — one person, many spouses. - Endogamy — marriage within the same group (caste, religion). - Exogamy — marriage outside one's group. subject: Applied Sociology
text: In simple words Sociology is the study of society, social relationships and social institutions. It looks at how people live together in groups — family, community, caste, class — and how society shapes health, illness and health behaviour. While psychology studies the individual mind, sociology studies the group and the social forces around the person. Nurses meet patients from many social backgrounds. Understanding society helps a nurse give respectful, fair care and see why some people cannot get treatment easily. title: Social Organisation & Disorganisation
summary: Social organisation, social control, and social disorganisation such as crime and family breakdown.
subject: Applied Sociology
text: In simple words Social organisation is a stable, orderly society where people know their roles and institutions work well. Social disorganisation is the breakdown of that order — when families, communities or institutions fail to support people. Disorganisation such as crime, family breakdown, unemployment or migration can harm health and make nursing care harder. Agents of social control These keep society orderly: - Family — teaches norms from childhood. - School — teaches rules and roles. - Religion — gives moral guidance. - Law and police — enforce rules. - Media — shows what is accepted. Social disorganisation Causes: poverty, unemployment, rapid urbanisation, migration, family breakdown, war, natural disasters. Effects: crime, substance abuse, neglect of children and elders, poor mental health, less access to care. Health effects People in disorganised communities may live in unsafe housing, eat poorly, delay treatment and miss follow-up. Nurses should assess social support and link patients with welfare services. title: Social Stratification
summary: Social stratification — caste, class, gender and inequality — and how they affect access to health care.
subject: Applied Sociology
text: In simple words Social stratification is the division of society into layers or strata based on caste, class, gender, race or religion. People in higher strata usually have more money, power and access to health care. Stratification is unequal and often passes from one generation to the next. It creates differences in health and life expectancy. Social mobility Social mobility is movement between strata — up or down. Education and jobs are the main routes upward in India. summary: Social structure, status and role, groups, institutions and how they influence health behaviour.
subject: Applied Sociology
text: In simple words Social structure is the organised pattern of relationships and institutions that make up a society. It includes status (position), role (expected behaviour), groups and institutions such as family, education and health care. A person's position in the social structure affects their access to food, housing, education and health care — and therefore their health. title: What is Communication?
summary: What communication is, its process, types and why it matters in nursing.
subject: Communicative English
text: In simple words Communication is the exchange of information, ideas and feelings between people. It can be through words (verbal) or without words (non-verbal). Good communication builds trust, helps assessment, and makes care safer. Poor communication causes errors, misunderstanding and complaints. title: Integrated LSRW Skills
summary: Using listening, speaking, reading and writing together in real nursing situations.
subject: Communicative English
text: In simple words In real nursing, you do not use one skill at a time. You listen to the patient, speak to explain, read the chart and write notes — all together. This is integrated LSRW. title: Attentive Listening
summary: What attentive listening is, its types, barriers and how to listen well to patients.
subject: Communicative English
text: In simple words Listening is not the same as hearing. Hearing is just sound reaching the ear; listening is paying attention and understanding. Attentive listening means focusing fully on the speaker, showing you are listening, and checking that you understood. It makes patients feel respected and helps you gather accurate information. Types of listening Type Meaning Nursing example --- --- --- Attentive Fully focused Listening to a patient's pain history Casual Relaxed, not detailed Chatting during a break Selective Hearing only parts Hearing only the words you expect Empathic Listening with feeling Listening to a patient's fears Barriers to listening - Noise and interruptions. - Thinking of your reply instead of listening. - Prejudice or assumptions about the patient. - Language difference. - Being tired or rushed. How to listen well - Face the patient and make eye contact. - Do not interrupt. - Use nods and small sounds ("mm-hmm"). - Repeat back what you heard ("So you mean the pain started last night?"). - Watch body language and feelings, not only words. subject: Communicative English
text: In simple words LSRW stands for Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing — the four skills of using a language. title: Reading Skills

subject: Communicative English
text: In simple words Reading is understanding written text. Nurses read charts, doctor's orders, medicine labels, reports and health education materials. Different situations need different reading styles — skimming for the main idea, scanning for a fact, and careful reading for instructions. title: Speaking & Effective Conversation
summary: Speaking clearly, tone, pronunciation, and effective patient conversation.
subject: Communicative English
text: In simple words Speaking is sharing information through words. Clear speaking means using simple words, speaking at the right speed, with the right tone and pronunciation. In nursing, how you say something matters as much as what you say. A calm, respectful tone helps a frightened patient feel safe. Features of clear speaking Feature What it means --- --- Simple words Use words the patient knows Right speed Not too fast, not too slow Clear pronunciation Say each word correctly Polite tone Respectful and calm Pauses Give the patient time to understand Effective conversation with a patient - Greet the patient and introduce yourself. - Explain what you are going to do before you do it. - Ask open questions ("How does the pain feel?"). - Listen to the answer before speaking again. - Thank the patient at the end. subject: Nursing Foundation I

subject: Nursing Foundation I
text: In simple words The nurse–patient relationship is a professional, trusting relationship built to help the patient meet health goals. It is different from a friendship — it has boundaries and a purpose. Communication is the heart of this relationship. Good communication helps assessment, teaching and comfort. title: Health & Illness

subject: Nursing Foundation I
text: In simple words Health is not just the absence of disease. The World Health Organization defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being. Illness is a state in which a person's normal functioning is reduced — physically, mentally or socially. A person can have a disease but still feel healthy, or feel ill without a diagnosed disease. Health and illness lie on a continuum — people move along it every day depending on their situation. subject: Nursing Foundation I
text: In simple words Health care delivery is how health services are organised and given to people. title: History of Nursing & Nursing as a Profession

subject: Nursing Foundation I
text: In simple words Modern nursing began with Florence Nightingale during the Crimean War (1854–56). She showed that cleanliness, fresh air and good care reduce death, and she started the first nursing school. In India, nursing began with missionary and government efforts, and the Indian Nursing Council (INC) was set up in 1947 to regulate nursing education and practice. Nursing is a profession because it has specialised knowledge, formal education, a code of ethics, a professional organisation and service to society. title: Promoting Safety in Health Care + First Aid
summary: Patient safety, fall prevention, fire safety and first aid for common emergencies.
subject: Nursing Foundation I
text: In simple words Patient safety means preventing harm to patients — falls, infections, medication errors and injuries. Nurses are the first line of safety. First aid is the immediate care given before professional help arrives. It preserves life, prevents worsening and promotes recovery. Patient safety - Fall prevention — keep the call bell within reach, non-slip footwear, uncluttered floor, good lighting, assist with walking. - Medication safety — right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time (the five rights). - Fire safety — RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish. subject: Applied Biochemistry
text: In simple words Acid–base balance keeps the blood pH in a narrow range. The normal blood pH is 7.35–7.45 . Below 7.35 is acidosis; above 7.45 is alkalosis. The body uses buffers, the lungs and the kidneys to keep pH steady. Even small changes affect enzyme work and cell function. subject: Applied Biochemistry
text: In simple words Carbohydrates are the body’s main source of energy. They are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and are broken down into glucose, which cells use for fuel. Carbohydrates come in three sizes: monosaccharides (single sugar), disaccharides (two sugars) and polysaccharides (many sugars). Most dietary carbohydrate is digested to glucose and absorbed into the blood. text: In simple words Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in the body. When cells are injured or die, enzymes leak into the blood. title: Heme Catabolism & Jaundice
summary: Heme breakdown, bilirubin formation and excretion, and types of jaundice.
subject: Applied Biochemistry
text: In simple words When red blood cells die, their haemoglobin is broken down. The haem part becomes bilirubin, which the liver processes and excretes in bile. If this pathway is blocked or overloaded, bilirubin builds up and causes jaundice (yellow skin and eyes). Normal serum bilirubin is about 0.3–1.2 mg/dL . Heme breakdown pathway 1. Red blood cell breakdown — haemoglobin splits into globin and haem. 2. Haem to biliverdin — haem is converted to biliverdin. 3. Biliverdin to bilirubin — unconjugated bilirubin forms. 4. Transport — unconjugated bilirubin binds albumin and travels to the liver. 5. Conjugation — liver adds glucuronic acid to make conjugated (direct) bilirubin. 6. Excretion — conjugated bilirubin goes into bile → intestine → faeces (urobilinogen, stercobilin). summary: Immunoglobulins — types, structure, functions and clinical significance.
subject: Applied Biochemistry
text: In simple words Immunoglobulins (antibodies) are Y-shaped proteins made by plasma cells. They bind to foreign substances (antigens) and help destroy them. They are the basis of humoral immunity. There are five main classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD. Each has a different role and location in the body. Classes of immunoglobulins Type Main location Main function --- --- --- IgG Blood, tissues Most abundant; crosses placenta; long-term protection IgA Secretions — saliva, tears, breast milk, gut Protects mucosal surfaces IgM Blood First antibody in response; largest IgE Skin, lungs, gut Allergy and parasite defence IgD B cell surface B cell receptor Structure and function An antibody has: - Two heavy chains and two light chains. - Two antigen-binding sites (the tips of the Y). - A constant region (the stem) that determines the class and effector function. Functions: - Neutralise toxins and viruses. - Opsonise bacteria for phagocytosis. - Activate complement. - Cross placenta (IgG only) to protect the newborn. subject: Applied Biochemistry
text: In simple words Lipids are fats and fat-like substances. They provide energy, form cell membranes, carry fat-soluble vitamins and make hormones. Excess lipid in the blood (hyperlipidaemia) increases the risk of atherosclerosis and heart disease. Lipids are digested slowly and need bile for emulsification and lipase for breakdown. Digestion and absorption Fat digestion is minimal in the stomach. subject: Applied Biochemistry
text: In simple words Proteins are made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. They build and repair tissues, make enzymes, hormones and antibodies, and maintain fluid balance. Protein is digested in the stomach by pepsin and in the small intestine by pancreatic proteases and brush-border enzymes. Amino acids are absorbed into the blood. subject: Applied Nutrition & Dietetics

text: In simple words Carbohydrates are the body’s cheapest and main source of energy. One gram gives about 4 kilocalories (kcal) . title: Cookery Rules & Food Preservation
summary: Cooking methods, nutrient loss during cooking, and food preservation methods.
subject: Applied Nutrition & Dietetics
text: In simple words Cooking makes food safe, tasty and digestible, but it can also destroy nutrients. Using the right cooking methods preserves nutrients. Food preservation keeps food safe to eat for longer by stopping or slowing the growth of microbes. Cooking methods Method Effect on nutrients --- --- Steaming Best; minimal nutrient loss Pressure cooking Good; fast, less water Boiling Some water-soluble vitamins lost Frying Adds fat; some nutrient loss Roasting/Baking Some vitamin loss Minimizing nutrient loss - Wash vegetables before cutting, not after. - Cut into large pieces; cook soon after cutting. - Use minimum water; do not overcook. - Use the cooking water in soups or gravies (it contains leached vitamins). - Avoid adding baking soda to vegetables (destroys vitamin C). Food preservation methods - Drying/sun-drying — removes water; microbes cannot grow. - Refrigeration — slows microbial growth. - Freezing — stops most microbial growth. - Canning — heat-sealed; long shelf life. - Salting and sugaring — draw out water; preserve. - Pasteurization — heat treatment of milk to kill germs. title: Fats
summary: Fats — types, sources, functions, essential fatty acids and role in health.
subject: Applied Nutrition & Dietetics
text: In simple words Fats are a concentrated source of energy. One gram of fat gives about 9 kcal — more than twice that of carbohydrates or protein. Fats also form cell membranes, carry fat-soluble vitamins and make hormones. Fats are classified as saturated, unsaturated and trans fats. Saturated and trans fats raise heart disease risk; unsaturated fats are healthier. Types of fats Type Examples Health effect --- --- --- Saturated Ghee, butter, coconut oil, red meat Raise blood cholesterol Unsaturated Vegetable oils, fish, nuts Generally healthier Trans Vanaspati, fried snacks, baked goods Worst for heart health Functions - Concentrated energy (9 kcal per gram). - Form cell membranes and nerve sheaths. - Carry fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. - Make hormones. - Insulate and protect organs. text: In simple words Food safety means handling, preparing and storing food so that it does not cause illness. Unsafe food can carry germs and cause diarrhoea, vomiting and food poisoning. They improve legibility, access and sharing of patient information — but they must be used carefully to protect privacy. Privacy and security - Access only records of patients in your care. - Do not share passwords. - Log off or lock the computer when away. - Report privacy breaches immediately. - Follow hospital policy and data-protection law. subject: Health / Nursing Informatics & Technology
text: In simple words Health information systems (HIS) are computer systems that manage health data in hospitals and clinics. They connect departments and improve care coordination. Key systems: hospital information system (HIS), electronic health record (EHR), picture archiving (PACS), radiology information (RIS), laboratory information (LIS). title: Information Law & Governance
summary: Information law — confidentiality, consent, data protection and health records governance.
subject: Health / Nursing Informatics & Technology
text: In simple terms Information law and governance protect patient information — who can see it, how it is used and how long it is kept. Confidentiality is a core duty of nurses. Key laws and principles: consent, data protection, confidentiality and records retention. Confidentiality and consent - Confidentiality: do not share patient information without permission or legal authority. - Consent: get permission before sharing information or using it for purposes other than care. - Minimum necessary: share only what is needed for the purpose. Data protection and governance - Store records securely (locked cabinets, password-protected computers). - Keep records for the required retention period. - Dispose of records securely (shredding, secure deletion). - Report breaches immediately. - Follow hospital policy and applicable data-protection law. subject: Health / Nursing Informatics & Technology
text: In simple words Health information management is the organisation, storage and use of health data and records. Good information management means data is accurate, complete and available when needed. Managers use information to make decisions about staffing, budgets, quality and services. title: Patient Safety & Clinical Risk
summary: Patient safety — goals, error prevention, reporting and a culture of safety.
subject: Health / Nursing Informatics & Technology
text: In simple words Patient safety means preventing harm to patients during care. Errors can happen — the goal is to build systems that catch them before they reach the patient. A culture of safety encourages reporting and learning from errors rather than blaming individuals. subject: Health / Nursing Informatics & Technology

title: Cultural Diversity
summary: Cultural diversity — cultural competence, beliefs affecting health, and culturally sensitive care.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Cultural diversity means people differ in culture, religion, language, food and beliefs. Culturally competent care respects these differences and adapts care to each patient’s culture. Culture affects health beliefs, diet, modesty, family roles, pain expression and decision-making. Culturally sensitive care - Ask about cultural and religious beliefs. - Respect dietary restrictions (fasting, vegetarian, halal, kosher). - Respect modesty — offer same-gender care when possible. - Use interpreters when language differs; do not use children. - Involve the family if the patient’s culture makes decisions as a family. title: Diagnostic Testing
summary: Diagnostic tests — blood, urine, ECG, X-ray, CT, MRI; nurse's role in preparation and aftercare.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Diagnostic tests help diagnose disease, plan treatment and monitor progress. Nurses prepare patients, explain procedures, collect samples and monitor after the test. Common tests: blood tests, urine tests, ECG, X-ray, CT scan, MRI, endoscopy. Common diagnostic tests Test Purpose Key preparation --- --- --- Blood glucose Sugar level Fasting for fasting glucose ECG Heart activity Lie still; remove metal X-ray Bones, chest Remove jewellery; pregnancy check CT scan Cross-sectional images Contrast allergy check MRI Detailed soft tissue Remove metal; claustrophobia check Urine routine Infection, kidney Clean-catch sample Nurse’s role - Before — explain the test, get consent, prepare the patient (fasting, contrast consent). - During — assist, monitor, comfort the patient. - After — monitor for reactions, remove IV, encourage fluids after contrast, report results. title: Elimination Needs
summary: Urinary and bowel elimination — normal patterns, assisting with elimination, and common problems.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Elimination is the removal of body waste — urine and faeces. Nurses help patients who cannot eliminate independently and observe for abnormalities. Normal urinary output is about 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour. Normal bowel pattern varies — from 3 times a day to 3 times a week. Normal patterns Elimination Normal pattern --- --- Urination 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour; pale yellow urine Bowel movement 3 times/day to 3 times/week; formed stool Assisting with elimination - Bedpan/urinal — offer regularly; position correctly; provide privacy. - Urinary catheter — insert as prescribed; keep bag below bladder; maintain asepsis. - Toilet/commode — assist mobile patients; use grab bars. - Enema — give as prescribed for constipation or bowel preparation. Common problems - Retention — unable to empty bladder; report; may need catheterisation. - Incontinence — involuntary loss; protect skin; use pads; toilet regularly. - Constipation — hard, infrequent stools; fluids, fibre, mobility. - Diarrhoea — frequent loose stools; prevent dehydration; record amount and character. title: Fluid, Electrolyte & Acid–Base Balance
summary: Fluid and electrolyte balance — IV fluids, electrolytes, imbalance signs and correction.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Fluid and electrolyte balance keeps the body’s water and salts at the right levels. IV fluids replace lost fluid and electrolytes. Imbalances can cause serious problems and must be corrected quickly. Fluid is inside cells (intracellular) and outside cells (extracellular — blood plasma and interstitial fluid). Common IV fluids Fluid Type Use --- --- --- Normal saline 0.9% Isotonic Dehydration, blood loss Dextrose 5% Isotonic (becomes hypotonic) Provides water, some energy Ringer’s lactate Isotonic Dehydration, shock, burns Dextrose saline Isotonic Dehydration + energy Electrolytes Electrolyte Normal value Main role --- --- --- Sodium (Na+) 135–145 mEq/L Fluid balance, nerve impulses Potassium (K+) 3.5–5.0 mEq/L Heart rhythm, muscle contraction Calcium (Ca2+) 8.5–10.5 mg/dL Bones, clotting, muscle Magnesium (Mg2+) 1.7–2.5 mEq/L Enzyme function, heart Imbalance signs - Hyperkalaemia (high K+) — dangerous heart rhythm changes; watch ECG. - Hypokalaemia (low K+) — weakness, constipation, heart rhythm changes. - Hyponatraemia (low Na+) — confusion, seizures. - Dehydration — dry mouth, poor skin turgor, low urine output. title: Health Assessment

subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Health assessment is the systematic collection of information about a patient’s health. It is the first step of the nursing process and guides all nursing care. Assessment gives a baseline, identifies health problems and helps plan care. It is continuous throughout hospitalization. Methods of assessment Method What it is Example --- --- --- Inspection Looking Skin colour, wounds Palpation Feeling Pulse, tenderness Percussion Tapping Lung density Auscultation Listening Heart and bowel sounds Components - Health history — present illness, past history, family history, lifestyle. - Physical examination — head to toe, systematic. - Vital signs — temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure, SpO2. - Psychosocial — mood, support, coping, culture. title: Hygiene & Pressure Ulcer Care
summary: Personal hygiene, oral care, hair care, nail care and pressure ulcer prevention and staging.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Hygiene keeps the patient clean, comfortable and prevents infection. It includes oral care, hair care, nail care, skin care and bathing. Pressure ulcers (bedsores) develop from prolonged pressure on skin, especially over bony areas. Prevention is easier than treatment. Pressure ulcer stages Stage Appearance --- --- Stage 1 Redness that does not blanch Stage 2 Partial-thickness skin loss (blister or shallow crater) Stage 3 Full-thickness skin loss (deep crater) Stage 4 Tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon or muscle Common pressure points - Sacrum, heels, elbows, hips, back of head, shoulders, ankles. Prevention - Turn the patient every 2 hours. - Use pressure-relieving mattresses and cushions. - Keep skin clean and dry; avoid moisture. - Massage is NOT recommended over red areas. - Check skin at least twice daily. title: Administration of Medications
summary: Medication administration — rights, routes, safety and the nurse's responsibilities.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Medication administration is giving prescribed drugs safely and correctly. Errors can harm or even kill patients, so strict checking is essential. The nurse checks the prescription, prepares the drug, gives it by the right route, observes the patient and documents everything. Rights of medication administration Right What to check --- --- Right patient Name and ID band Right drug Name matches prescription Right dose Correct amount and calculation Right route Oral, IV, IM, subcutaneous, etc. Right time Correct time and frequency Right reason Why the drug is given Right documentation Record after giving Common routes Route Examples Notes --- --- --- Oral Tablets, syrups Safest, most common Intravenous (IV) Injection, infusion Fast action; monitor closely Intramuscular (IM) Into muscle Vaccines, some antibiotics Subcutaneous Under skin Insulin, heparin Topical Creams, ointments Local effect Medication safety - Check the label three times: when taking from storage, before pouring, before giving. - Do not leave medications unattended. - Calculate doses carefully; have another nurse check high-risk doses. - Report errors immediately — do not hide them. - Watch for allergi

title: The Nursing Process
summary: The nursing process — assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation (ADPIE).
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words The nursing process is a systematic, scientific way to give nursing care. It has five steps: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation — remembered as ADPIE . It is cyclical — after evaluation, you reassess and start again. It ensures care is individualised and effective. The five steps Step What the nurse does --- --- Assessment Collects data about the patient Diagnosis Identifies actual or potential health problems Planning Sets goals and chooses interventions Implementation Carries out the planned care Evaluation Checks whether goals were met Example A patient with fever: - Assess: temperature 39°C, flushed skin. - Diagnose: hyperthermia related to infection. - Plan: reduce temperature within 2 hours. - Implement: tepid sponging, antipyretic as ordered, fluids. - Evaluate: recheck temperature; if normal, goal met. ADPIE cycle Assess Diagnose Plan Implement Evaluate Cyclical — evaluate, then reassess Individualised care Scientific method Outcome focused Assessment → Diagnosis → Planning → Implementation → Evaluation. title: Nursing Theories

subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Nursing theories give a framework for understanding what nurses do and why. They guide assessment, care planning and evaluation. title: Nutritional Needs
summary: Nutritional needs — balanced diet, therapeutic diets, assessing nutritional status and feeding methods.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Nutrition is essential for health, growth, healing and immunity. Nurses assess nutritional status, plan diets and help patients eat. A balanced diet gives all nutrients in correct amounts. Patients who cannot eat normally may need tube feeding or intravenous fluids. Components of a balanced diet Food group Examples Function --- --- --- Cereals Rice, wheat, ragi Energy Pulses Dal, beans, soya Protein Milk and products Milk, curd, paneer Calcium, protein Vegetables and fruits Seasonal produce Vitamins, minerals, fibre Fats and oils Oil, ghee, nuts Energy, fat-soluble vitamins Water Drinking water Transport, temperature Feeding methods - Oral feeding — normal eating; assist weak patients. - Spoon feeding — for patients who cannot hold a spoon. - Tube feeding — nasogastric or gastrostomy tube; as prescribed. - Intravenous fluids — when the gut cannot be used; strictly as prescribed. title: Oxygenation Needs
summary: Oxygenation — oxygen therapy, delivery devices, suctioning and chest physiotherapy.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Oxygenation is the process of getting oxygen into the blood and tissues. Patients with breathing problems may need oxygen therapy, suctioning or chest physiotherapy. Oxygen is a drug — it must be given as prescribed, with the right flow rate and device. Oxygen delivery devices Device Flow rate Use --- --- --- Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min Mild hypoxia, long-term Simple face mask 5–10 L/min Moderate hypoxia Venturi mask Fixed % Precise oxygen concentration Non-rebreather mask 10–15 L/min Severe hypoxia Normal SpO2: 95–100% . Give oxygen as prescribed; do not change flow without orders. Suctioning Suction removes secretions from the mouth, nose or airway when the patient cannot cough. Use asepsis, pre-oxygenate, suction for less than 15 seconds, and monitor. Chest physiotherapy - Percussion — clapping over lung segments to loosen mucus. - Vibration — gentle shaking during expiration. - Postural drainage — positions to drain specific lung areas. - Helps after surgery, in pneumonia and COPD. title: Self-Concept
summary: Self-concept — self-esteem, body image, role performance and factors affecting self-concept.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Self-concept is how a person sees themselves — self-esteem, body image and role. Illness, injury and hospitalisation can damage self-concept. Nurses support self-concept by respecting the patient, encouraging independence and promoting a positive body image. Components of self-concept Component Meaning --- --- Self-esteem How much a person values themselves Body image How a person sees their own body Role performance How well a person performs their roles (parent, worker) Personal identity Who a person believes they are Factors affecting self-concept - Illness, injury, disability. - Surgery (mastectomy, amputation, stoma). - Ageing, pregnancy, menopause. - Culture, religion, social status. - Criticism or praise from others. title: Sensory Needs
summary: Sensory needs — sensory deprivation and overload, assessment and nursing care.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Sensory needs are the need for input from sight, sound, touch, taste and smell. Too little stimulation (sensory deprivation) or too much (sensory overload) can cause confusion, anxiety and distress. Hospital patients are at risk — isolation, tubes, monitors and restricted movement affect sensory input. Sensory deprivation vs overload Type Cause Signs --- --- --- Sensory deprivation Too little input Confusion, hallucinations, boredom, restlessness Sensory overload Too much input Irritability, anxiety, inability to focus, fatigue Nursing care - Sensory deprivation — provide stimulation: talk, read, television, visitors, change of position, window view. - Sensory overload — reduce stimulation: dim lights, lower noise, limit visitors, rest periods. - Assess — hearing, vision, speech, response to stimuli. - Communication — speak clearly, face the patient, check understanding. title: Sexuality
summary: Sexuality — sexual health across lifespan, illness effects, and nurse's role in discussing sexuality.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Sexuality is a core part of being human — it includes gender identity, sexual orientation, intimacy, relationships and reproduction. It continues throughout life, including during illness and older age. Illness, surgery, medicines and hospitalisation can affect sexuality. Nurses should address sexuality with respect, privacy and without judgement. Sexuality across the lifespan Stage Focus --- --- Childhood Learning about body and privacy Adolescence Puberty, identity, relationships Adulthood Intimacy, reproduction, relationships Older age Continued intimacy; may need adaptation Effects of illness on sexuality - Surgery (mastectomy, hysterectomy, prostate surgery) — body image changes. - Medicines — may reduce libido or cause erectile dysfunction. - Pain, fatigue and anxiety — reduce sexual interest. - Disability — may need positioning aids or new ways of intimacy. Nurse’s role - Provide privacy for couples. - Answer questions honestly and respectfully. - Do not assume all patients are heterosexual — avoid assumptions. - Refer to counsellors or doctors when needed. - Keep information confidential. title: Stress & Adaptation
summary: Stress — causes, general adaptation syndrome, coping and adaptation to illness.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Stress is the body’s response to any demand or threat. A stressor is anything that causes stress — illness, pain, hospitalisation, noise, worry. The body responds through the general adaptation syndrome (GAS): alarm, resistance and exhaustion. Coping helps the person adapt. General adaptation syndrome (Selye) Stage What happens --- --- Alarm “Fight or flight” — heart rate up, adrenaline Resistance Body adapts; coping continues Exhaustion Resources depleted; illness or burnout Coping strategies - Problem-focused — tackle the cause directly. - Emotion-focused — manage the feelings (talk, pray, relax). - Adaptation — adjusting to a new health state (e.g., living with diabetes). Nurse’s role - Identify stressors and help reduce them. - Teach relaxation — deep breathing, music, rest. - Support coping — listen, involve family, encourage. - Watch for exhaustion — burnout in patients and staff. General adaptation syndrome Alarm Resistance Exhaustion Coping Problem-focused Emotion-focused Adaptation Prolonged stress leads to exhaustion — illness, burnout or breakdown. Recognise early and support coping before it reaches this stage. Where the nurse uses this - Identify stress

title: Care of the Terminally Ill, Death & Dying
summary: Terminal care — palliative care, signs of approaching death, care after death and grief support.
subject: Nursing Foundation II
text: In simple words Terminal care is care for patients who are dying. The goal is comfort, dignity and relief from pain and distress — not cure. This is palliative care. Nurses support the patient and family through dying and after death, including grief support. Signs of approaching death - Decreased consciousness, more sleeping. - Breathing changes (Cheyne–Stokes, long pauses). - Cool hands and feet; mottled skin. - Reduced intake of food and fluids. - Loss of bladder and bowel control. Care after death - Close the eyes; straighten the limbs. - Wash and dress the body; position respectfully. - Label the body correctly. - Support the family; allow time with the body. - Follow hospital and legal procedures (death certificate, autopsy consent). Grief support - Listen; allow the family to express feelings. - Do not say “I know how you feel.” - Provide privacy and time. - Refer to counselling if needed. title: Blood Disorders
summary: Blood disorders — anaemia, leukaemia, clotting disorders, thrombocytopenia — nursing care.
subject: Adult Health Nursing I
text: In simple terms Blood disorders affect the blood cells or clotting system — anaemia (low red cells/haemoglobin), leukaemia (cancer of white cells), and bleeding/clotting disorders. Nurses monitor blood counts, give transfusions and prevent bleeding. title: Cardiovascular Disorders
summary: Cardiovascular disorders — hypertension, angina, MI, heart failure, arrhythmias — nursing care.
subject: Adult Health Nursing I
text: In simple words Cardiovascular disorders affect the heart and blood vessels — hypertension, angina, myocardial infarction (heart attack), heart failure and arrhythmias. Nurses monitor vital signs, give medications, and teach lifestyle changes. Common cardiovascular disorders Disorder Cause/Features Key signs --- --- --- Hypertension Persistently high BP Often silent; headache, dizziness Angina Coronary artery narrowing Chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest/GTN Myocardial infarction (MI) Coronary artery blockage; heart muscle death Severe chest pain, sweating, nausea, breathlessness Heart failure Heart can't pump effectively Breathlessness, oedema, fatigue, crackles Arrhythmias Irregular rhythm Palpitations, dizziness, syncope Nursing care - Hypertension — monitor BP, give antihypertensives as ordered, teach salt restriction, weight control, medication compliance. - Angina — GTN sublingual for chest pain; sit patient down; rest; report unrelieved pain. - MI — emergency; oxygen, ECG, cardiac enzymes, thrombolysis/PCI as ordered; monitor for arrhythmias and complications. - Heart failure — daily weight, fluid/salt restriction, diuretics as ordered, position upright, monitor oedema

title: Common Signs & Symptoms: Shock, Pain, Fluids
summary: Common signs and symptoms — shock, pain, fluid imbalance — recognition and nursing care.
subject: Adult Health Nursing I
text: In simple words Nurses constantly assess for common signs and symptoms that signal a patient is deteriorating — shock, pain and fluid imbalance. Early recognition and action save lives. Shock is life-threatening — inadequate tissue perfusion. Pain is whatever the patient says it is. Fluid imbalance means too much or too little fluid. title: Communicable Diseases
summary: Communicable diseases — TB, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis, typhoid, malaria — transmission, prevention, nursing care.
subject: Adult Health Nursing I
text: In simple words Communicable diseases spread from person to person or from animals/environment to humans — TB, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis, typhoid, malaria, COVID-19, influenza. title: Introduction to Microbiology

subject: Applied Microbiology & Infection Control
text: In simple words Microbiology is the study of microorganisms — living things too small to be seen without a microscope. These include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths (worms). Some microbes are helpful (they help digest food and make vitamins); others cause disease (they are called pathogens). Nurses must understand microbes to prevent and control infection. Enter the body (portal of entry — skin break, airway, gut, blood). 2. Multiply in a suitable site. 3. Produce toxins or damage tissues. 4. Spread to other sites or people. The body defends itself through skin, mucus, stomach acid, white cells and antibodies. title: General Pathology

subject: Pathology I
text: In simple words Pathology is the study of disease — its causes, mechanisms, structural changes and effects on the body. General pathology covers the basic processes that underlie most diseases: cell injury, inflammation, healing and repair. Understanding these basics helps nurses understand what happens inside the body during illness. Cell injury Cells are injured by hypoxia (lack of oxygen), toxins, infections, physical agents (heat, cold, radiation) and immune reactions. - Reversible injury — cell can recover if the cause is removed (e.g., swelling, fatty change). - Irreversible injury — cell dies (necrosis or apoptosis). - Necrosis — cell death due to injury (swelling, rupture, inflammation). - Apoptosis — programmed cell death (normal, controlled, no inflammation). Inflammation Inflammation is the body's response to injury or infection — redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function (the 5 cardinal signs). - Acute inflammation — sudden, short-term (neutrophils dominant). - Chronic inflammation — long-term (lymphocytes and macrophages dominant). text: In simple words Five conditions cause most childhood illness in India: diarrhoea, pneumonia, measles, malnutrition and anaemia . subject: Child Health Nursing I
text: In simple words Children collapse mainly because of breathing problems , not heart problems. title: Introduction to Mental Health Nursing
summary: What mental health is, what mental illness is, the historical background and the scope of mental health nursing.
subject: Mental Health Nursing I
text: In simple words Mental health is not just the absence of mental illness. It is a state of balance in which a person can use his abilities, cope with normal stresses, work productively and contribute to the community. Mental illness is a disturbance of thinking, feeling, behaviour or perception that causes distress and interferes with daily life. Signs of positive mental health - Accepts self, has realistic self-respect - Forms warm and satisfying relationships - Can work, play and be productive - Copies with stress and frustration - Feels secure and accepted - Can make decisions and take responsibility Mental Health Nursing CHAPTER MAP 1 Mental health balance, coping and productive life 2 Mental illness distress and interference with daily life 3 Four levels of care promotion, prevention, treatment, rehabilitation 4 Where nurses work hospital, clinic, school, community, home A brief history of psychiatric nursing in India - 1745 to 1800 — lunatic asylums with custodial care (London, Bombay, Calcutta) - 1794 to 1858 — moral treatment began; restraint reduced - 1858 onwards — Lunacy Acts; Indian Lunacy Act 1912 - 1947 — Indian Psychiatric Society formed - 1987 — Mental Health Act 198

title: Mood Disorders

subject: Mental Health Nursing I
text: In simple words Mood disorders are illnesses in which mood is disturbed for weeks and interferes with life. Depression pulls the person down; mania pushes him up. Depression — symptoms - Low mood, most of the day, nearly every day - Loss of interest and pleasure (anhedonia) - Sleep changes — early morning waking (typical) - Appetite and weight change - Fatigue and tiredness - Poor concentration; indecisiveness - Worthlessness, guilt, helplessness - Thoughts of death and suicide - Low libido, constipation, psychomotor slowing Diagnosis: symptoms for over 2 weeks with functional impairment. title: Schizophrenia & Psychotic Disorders
summary: Schizophrenia — symptoms, types, causes, treatment and the nursing care of psychotic patients.
subject: Mental Health Nursing I
text: In simple words Schizophrenia is a chronic mental illness that affects thinking, feeling and behaviour. The patient loses contact with reality. It usually starts in late adolescence or early adulthood, and with treatment many people lead useful lives. It is not split personality, and it is not madness in the film sense. text: In simple words A psychiatric emergency needs immediate action to protect life and safety. The first priorities are always safety, airway, breathing and circulation , then the mental state. subject: Midwifery / OBG Nursing I
text: In simple words The newborn is in a period of rapid adjustment. Good care means airway, warmth, cord and eye care, safe feeding and early identification of problems. subject: Midwifery / OBG Nursing I
text: In simple words The puerperium is the 6 weeks after delivery. During this period the uterus returns to its normal state (involution), lactation begins and the mother recovers.
